one_liner: Rust SIMD non-cryptographic 64/128-bit hash with a C99 port. First-party Zen 4 numbers show 1.5-2.2x xxh3 at 1-64 KiB, but it is slower on tiny keys.
what_it_does: A Rust crate (with an in-repo C99 port and wasm bindings) that exposes two unrelated hash functions behind one API. The default `lanehash` needs no special instructions and gives bit-identical output on the scalar, SSE2, AVX2, AVX-512, NEON and wasm SIMD128 backends. `lanehash::aes` is the original 0.1 AES-lane function. Both provide `hash64(bytes, seed)` / `hash128`, an incremental `Stream` that matches the one-shot result, and `FixedState` / `RandomState` BuildHashers for `HashMap`; the AES variant adds `hash64_batch`. The API has the same shape as seeded xxh3, but the outputs differ, so persisted xxh3 values cannot be migrated.
how_it_is_fast: Inputs over 64 bytes are split into 64-byte stripes dealt round-robin to 8 independent chains of 8 64-bit lanes (512-byte blocks). Each lane step is an NH-32-style `x = A ^ w; A = x + lo32(x) * hi32(x)`, a 32x32->64 multiply that maps onto vector multiply units. Sixty-four independent lanes keep AVX-512/AVX2 pipelines busy and hide multiply latency. The lanes are merged with one extra step per chain and finished with 64x64->128 multiply-folds. Inputs of 0-64 bytes use a scalar wyhash/rapidhash-style 'protected mum' multiply-fold path. The AES variant replaces the lane step with AESENC rounds (two lanes per ymm with VAES), and the backend is detected once and cached in an atomic.
when_to_use: Rust bulk hashing of 1 KiB-1 MiB buffers on x86-64 with AVX2/AVX-512: first-party Zen 4 numbers are 13.6 / 21.8 / 27.0 bytes/cycle at 1 / 4 / 64 KiB, against 6.3 / 12.8 / 18.5 for xxh3
Medium keys around 256 B in throughput mode: 42-45 cycles/hash vs 101 for xxh3 and 72 for rapidhash v3 on the same Ryzen 5 7600

Checksums or dedup keys that must be identical across x86, aarch64, wasm and C. Every backend and the C port are differentially tested against the scalar reference, and hash128 did 4 KiB page dedup in 526 cycles/page vs 588 for xxh3-128
Maximum bulk speed on VAES CPUs (Zen 4 class) via `lanehash::aes`: rurban SMHasher EPYC 9554P shows 107,602 MiB/s vs xxh3 45,762
A general Rust HashMap hasher: the author's map workloads show roughly half of std SipHash-1-3's cycles per op and parity with foldhash/rapidhash on string keys
when_not_to_use: Tiny keys: at 4-16 B it takes 11.4-12.0 cycles/hash vs 9.5-10.1 for xxh3 in throughput mode, and 25.4 vs 23.5 cycles for rapidhash v3 in dependent-chain latency
Latency-bound keys of 65-128 B: they switch to the long path, and latency-final.csv shows 70.6 cycles at 128 B vs 39.7 for xxh3 and 44.1 for rapidhash v3
DRAM-bound streaming such as big-file checksums: the README reports a 64 MiB checksum at 45.8 GB/s, below xxh3's 50.9 and gxhash's 49.9

Production code that needs a mature, reviewed format. The repo was created 2026-09-18 and has 1 star and one author, the crate-root algorithm was swapped a week later, 0.2.0 is still 'unreleased', and quality evidence is statistical only (SMHasher, SMHasher3, Miri) with no security claims

Scalar-only targets, or no_std builds without target-feature flags. Scalar execution is 'substantially slower', no_std x86-64 picks the backend at compile time only (SSE2 by default, about 14.5 B/cycle at 64 KiB), and the C port has no NEON backend

integration.dependencies: none at runtime (libc is a dev-dependency); an optional self-contained C99 source-drop lives in lanehash-c/
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.89 (edition 2021); the C port is C99 for GCC/clang, with unsigned __int128 optional via LANEHASH_NO_INT128
integration.platforms: Any Rust target. SIMD backends: x86-64 SSE2/AVX2/AVX-512F (runtime-detected with std), aarch64 NEON, wasm32 SIMD128. The AES variant uses AES-NI/VAES/Armv8 AES, or T-table software AES elsewhere. The C port picks x86 SIMD at compile time and uses scalar code elsewhere.
integration.thread_safety: One-shot functions are pure. The chosen backend is cached in an AtomicUsize and RandomState's per-process seed in a OnceLock. Stream and LaneHasher are ordinary owned values with no further documented guarantees.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the API shape matches seeded xxh3 (64/128-bit one-shot, streaming, BuildHasher), but the outputs differ, so it cannot replace stored xxh3 hashes

gotchas: Version mismatch: the README says `lanehash = "0.2"`, but crates.io only has 0.1.0 (2026-09-18, 15 downloads), whose crate root is the AES function. 0.2 changes the output of `lanehash::hash64`, so use a git dependency or pin exactly and check the verification values (0xD048C22B default, 0x9FF60BEF AES).

Naming confusion: rurban SMHasher's `lanehash64`/`lanehash128` rows are the AES variant (verification 0x9FF60BEF, log header 'AES lanes + mum short path'). The repo now uses `lanehash64` for the new default and `lanehash_aes64` for AES, and 'lanehash' rows in docs/bench/TABLES.md also mean AES.
HashMap output (FixedState/RandomState via LaneHasher) is a different function from hash64 and may change between minor releases. Do not persist it.
Without hardware AES, the AES variant falls back to T-table software AES (data-indexed table lookups), which is much slower. Use the default algorithm on such targets.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over xxHash (xxh3) and rapidhash for 256 B-1 MiB buffers in Rust on AVX2/AVX-512 hardware, or when you need bit-identical results across x86, ARM, wasm and C. Pick it over gxhash when you cannot rely on AES, since the default algorithm needs none; with VAES, the AES variant only roughly ties gxhash (107,602 vs 103,530 MiB/s on EPYC 9554P).
verified_claims_summary: The first-party harness on a Ryzen 5 7600 (cargo release, fat LTO, AVX-512 dispatch, rustc unstated, xxh3 from the xxhash-rust 0.8.18 crate) measured the default algorithm at 27.0 vs 18.5 B/cycle at 64 KiB (+46%) and 21.8 vs 12.8 at 4 KiB, but slower below 32 B. The repo's separate C-reference run (gcc 13) puts upstream C xxh3 at about 13 B/cycle at 64 KiB, so the Rust-port baseline does not look weak. The only independent data is rurban SMHasher (CMake Release, -march=native, compiler unstated), and it covers only the AES variant: 107,602 vs 45,762 MiB/s for xxh3 on an EPYC 9554P (about 2.35x).
status_note: Brand new and in flux: created 2026-09-18, 1 star, last commit 2026-09-23, a breaking algorithm swap in its first week and 0.2.0 unpublished on crates.io. It is MIT OR Apache-2.0 with no dependencies, and the C99 port is small enough to vendor.
